title: Buyback and grant proposals are exempt from the 1% submission threshold, giving distributive proposals the lowest barrier to entry
content:
A.6.1.1.3.2.2.2.2.1.2.1.1.1 waives the 1% threshold "for proposals that solely entail a buyback or a grant of KEEL tokens," while stating that "all other procedural requirements within the Root Edit process continue to apply."

The carve-out inverts the usual intuition. Proposals that spend Keel's resources — buying back its own token, or granting tokens to someone — are exactly the class one might expect to gate most tightly, and instead they are the only class any holder can raise.

The rationale is legible from the structure of the rest of the process. The 1% bar exists to filter noise before human review time is spent, but it also concentrates the power to raise *capital-return* questions in the hands of the largest holders — the parties least likely to need it and most likely to have private channels. Removing the bar for buybacks and grants means a small holder can force the question of returning value to holders onto the public record, where the Operational Facilitator must review it and, if aligned, put it to a vote.

The protection against abuse is not the threshold but the remainder of the pipeline: alignment review, forum publication, quorum and the Artifact Edit Restrictions all still bind. Widening who may ask does not widen who may approve.
description: Any KEEL holder may propose a buyback or token grant regardless of size, while all other procedural requirements still apply — deliberately widening access to the proposals that move value to holders.
